definition: In the theory of Probably Approximately Correct Machine Learning, the Natarajan dimension characterizes the complexity of learning a set of functions, generalizing from the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension for boolean functions to multi-class functions.
details: Originally introduced as the Generalized Dimension by Natarajan, it was subsequently renamed the Natarajan Dimension by Haussler and Long.

explainer.lead: It measures how complex a multi-class function class is for learning, extending the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension beyond binary outputs. It matters because standard VC theory does not cover learners that must choose among many labels.

tiers.eli5: Think of how many different ways a sorting rule can group a handful of objects into several bins; the more groupings it can produce, the harder the rule is to learn.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to reason about generalization bounds for multi-class classifiers where the binary VC dimension does not apply. A pitfall is assuming binary VC-style intuition carries over directly to multi-class settings.
tiers.paperLevel: Generalizes the VC dimension from boolean to multi-class function classes; introduced by Natarajan as the Generalized Dimension and renamed by Haussler and Long. Its exact value can be hard to compute for large, unstructured function classes.

explainer.example: For a classifier that assigns each input one of k labels, the Natarajan dimension bounds how many distinct labelings it can realize on a sample and feeds into a generalization bound.
